title: Leading with AI: Strategies, Legal Insights, and Defining Key Terms — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source acknowledges that AI will reshape junior work and that effective use requires experience and judgment, but it does not develop the cluster’s central claim that automation may disrupt expertise reproduction. Instead, it prioritises involving associates in AI strategy, inclusive learning and practical experimentation.
qs: So I think, from a strategy standpoint, really accelerating your ability as an organization to move into the future requires that you engage with the associates.
And it turns out, based on this research with BCG consultants, that's not necessarily the case; you also need experience and judgment to know how best to deploy these technologies.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The excerpt promotes AI literacy through personal experimentation and records early impressions of ChatGPT’s convenience, but it does not assess court AI against unmet legal need, existing institutional failures, justice outcomes, or the cluster’s identified reliability and governance risks.
qs: We’re excited to create this project to help accelerate AI literacy in the legal profession.
It's nice to have an answer all put together instead of pulling from a bunch of different websites.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source promotes AI literacy and firsthand experimentation, but it does not address dispute-resolution process redesign, access to justice, or the central distinction between AI assistance and machine adjudication. Its personal impressions also provide no performance or legitimacy evidence.
qs: We’re excited to create this project to help accelerate AI literacy in the legal profession.
I was sort of doing some pretty basic prompts and thinking, Okay, yeah, this is kind of fun.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claims that AI will pressure junior-hour leverage and require business-model rethinking, while materially extending the implementation response: associates should be directly involved in AI strategy because their workflow knowledge can reveal use cases, efficiencies and new revenue opportunities. Its claims remain largely experiential and predictive rather than systematic evidence.
qs: And because of the nature of the work that junior lawyers do, they are more likely to identify use cases that an experienced securities lawyer may not be flagging—use cases that could create efficiencies or even open up new revenue streams for the firm that it hadn't thought of before.

That democratize piece, for really, really big global firms that are highly leveraged and rely on the generation of enormous amounts of billable hours at the junior levels in particular, will be impacted by this technology in ways that challenge their existing business model.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source accepts the practitioner-led case for engaging with AI before certainty and materially develops it by proposing organisation-wide baseline AI literacy and explicit involvement of junior lawyers whose work may be most affected. Its support rests mainly on practitioner observations and personal experience, not systematic outcome evidence.
qs: It might feel infantilizing to you that we're going to start here, but we can’t actually move forward with a conversation as an organization or a team without level-setting at the moment and then moving forward.
The associates don't really know how they should be involved, even though a lot of the technology will impact their work, maybe even more than senior attorneys' work.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts legal AI as organisational and service redesign, then materially develops the proposition through an adaptive, mission-aligned strategy and a concrete model of bottom-up learning involving associates and individual use-case experimentation. Its claims are mainly prescriptive and experiential rather than measured implementation evidence.
qs: But I think a smart thing to do as an organization is to work together to create a framework that represents a strategy aligned with your organization's goals and mission.

I think it's something for leaders to think about, because I can also understand busy partners saying, “We don't have the time to integrate all of this information and make sure that everybody's voice is heard.” But because this is such a weird technology, it also requires bottom-up learning.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI should be selectively managed within redesigned, human-led workflows rather than ignored or treated as wholesale lawyer replacement. It materially extends that proposition by advocating approved proprietary systems, policies and training to address covert use, and by identifying integration of public and internal legal information as a concrete driver of workflow and junior-role redesign. Its claims are mainly experiential and predictive rather than empirically demonstrated.
qs: And that carries with it much greater risk than any risk of having your team using it safely with guidance and teaching and training.

So, you know, one of the challenges ahead is really reshaping those roles that involve that activity—which I think will be exciting for a lot of people, to not have that be a major part of your job anymore and to really focus on the law itself.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source supports selective, manageable continuous learning rather than release chasing. It recommends curated commentary that avoids overload and explicitly values cross-industry perspectives for identifying implications for law, while offering personal recommendations rather than empirical validation.
qs: It will not overwhelm your inbox, and it's a great way to keep up with what he's working on and sort of aggregating.

(Ethan Mollick's content isn't explicitly legal either, but...) I've really enjoyed it for understanding how the technology is going to impact so many other parts of your life and your world—other industries—because that then helps me think about the corollaries in law.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s broad framing that AI will materially affect junior lawyers and requires deliberate organisational involvement, while adding associate uncertainty about their role in adoption. It does not directly establish weakened apprenticeship or succession routes, nor offer evidence on training effectiveness.
qs: The associates don't really know how they should be involved, even though a lot of the technology will impact their work, maybe even more than senior attorneys' work.
But I think the technology is going to allow so many new things that lawyers can do, that you want to get fully involved.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that AI value and impact depend on organisational engagement rather than access alone. It highlights firms’ business-model and client-engagement priorities and the need to involve associates whose work may be especially affected, while offering predictions and encouragement rather than measured implementation outcomes.
qs: And I think the red blinking light for a lot of firms in particular has been the business model and the client engagement piece.
The associates don't really know how they should be involved, even though a lot of the technology will impact their work, maybe even more than senior attorneys' work.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the engagement-first proposition by portraying AI as a potentially transformative capability for resource-constrained legal providers and by endorsing continual learning about law’s technological future. It also anticipates opportunities for courts and dispute-resolution institutions, though these are expectations rather than evidence-backed implementation proposals.
qs: You can start to do things you weren't capable of doing, and really compete and transform the way that law is practiced.

But your last point—and all of the, you know, "Avengers" of thinking about the future of law that we've referenced—one of the things I think is so cool about this moment, personally (and maybe it's just because of the way I like to learn), is that you're really foraging for information every day.

kp.k: Integrated knowledge systems could reshape research and associate tasks
kp.d: Leonard interprets the reported vLex–iManage partnership as an attempt to connect public legal research with firms’ accumulated internal work product, reducing repeated work and movement between systems. McCormack anticipates significant workflow and client-service effects. Leonard predicts that junior roles involving synthesis and aggregation across these sources will need reshaping; neither speaker presents measured outcomes from the partnership.
qs: But those two bodies of information have never really seen one another in a major way.
the ability not to reinvent the wheel every time, or have to exit one body and enter another and bring that information back and forth.
a lot of my experience as a junior associate was jumping in and out of these different bodies of information and synthesizing and aggregating a lot of it.

kp.k: Uneven capabilities require repeated, task-specific experimentation
kp.d: McCormack explains the 'jagged frontier' as unexpectedly uneven AI performance across tasks, drawing on Ethan Mollick’s blog rather than the underlying paper. She argues that disappointing initial attempts can discourage lawyers from discovering useful applications. Leonard adds that apparently conflicting assessments may reflect different prompts and tasks, recommending repeated testing as capabilities change. These are adoption interpretations, not reported legal-task benchmark results.
qs: I never read the actual paper.
Then there are other things that you would expect it to be good at that it's not very good at.
And the only way to figure it out is to push to the edge and see if it works.
they think they're arguing about the same experience when they're actually having a totally different conversation. And they both may be right.

kp.k: AI literacy varies within and across generations
kp.d: Leonard attributes the 'uneven law of AI distribution' to discussions by Paul Roetzer and Mike Kaput: professionals have different knowledge, experience and expectations, making shared baseline education necessary. McCormack reports encounters with senior lawyers relieved to retire rather than learn AI, but also observes differing enthusiasm among her twenty-something children. Both advocate inclusive, continuing learning rather than assuming age determines readiness.
qs: everybody is at a different place right now, at least in understanding what generative AI is, what its capabilities are, and what impact it will have on the world and our work.
we can’t actually move forward with a conversation as an organization or a team without level-setting at the moment and then moving forward.
Everybody's learning, and that's going to be true for a while.

kp.k: Junior familiarity with technology does not replace judgment
kp.d: Leonard reports research with BCG consultants, described as having appeared 'last week, I think,' as challenging the assumption that younger workers necessarily deploy generative AI wisely. She argues that experience and judgment remain important and that senior leaders should recognize their potential contribution. The transcript provides no study title, sample size or quantitative findings; the evidence discussed concerns consultants rather than lawyers.
qs: there is sort of this myth of the "digital native"—that just because you're younger, you will have a better understanding of how to deploy technology.
based on this research with BCG consultants, that's not necessarily the case; you also need experience and judgment to know how best to deploy these technologies.

kp.k: Undisclosed AI use undermines prohibition-based risk management
kp.d: McCormack uses 'secret cyborg' to describe employees using AI without organizational guidance, potentially on personal devices, despite leadership opposition. A conference conversation with a managing partner and nearby junior lawyers illustrates her concern, rather than establishing prevalence. She asserts that unguided use creates greater risk than trained, policy-compliant use. Leonard considers pressured juniors particularly understandable candidates for such behavior but explicitly says none has disclosed it to her.
qs: So the secret cyborg is those people in your organization that are using it—whether you have told them to or not
But they're using it without any guidance or instruction from you about how to use it in a way that complies with your other policies that are important to your business and your practice.
And that carries with it much greater risk than any risk of having your team using it safely with guidance and teaching and training.
I haven't had any secret cyborgs unveil themselves to me as a secret cyborg

kp.k: Risk managers may push firms toward internal GPT systems
kp.d: Leonard predicts, without a precise date or supporting insurance evidence, that malpractice insurers or risk managers will encourage or require internal proprietary GPT models to reduce unauthorized use. She also asserts that AI detection is unreliable. Her account of a partner taking a typo as evidence of human authorship is a reported anecdote, not an established detection method.
qs: I think we will very soon enter a world where malpractice insurers or risk managers are requiring or strongly encouraging organizations to create internal proprietary GPT models that people can use to avoid this.
AI detection technology is notoriously fallible and there's no real way for you to know whether a secret cyborg created something or an associate within your organization did.

kp.k: Associates should participate directly in AI strategy
kp.d: Leonard reports that associates want to know their organizations’ AI plans but lack clarity about involvement, despite potentially substantial effects on their work. McCormack, explicitly noting that she is neither an associate nor employed in a law firm, recommends volunteering for learning forums, use-case exploration, governance and innovation teams. She views this as an unusual opportunity for juniors to collaborate with senior lawyers outside established expertise hierarchies; Leonard suggests associates’ committees as a route into decision-making.
qs: The associates don't really know how they should be involved, even though a lot of the technology will impact their work, maybe even more than senior attorneys' work.
I am not an associate and I don't work in a law firm.
this is an opportunity for you and pretty senior people in your firm to work together and to get to know each other in a way that probably would be hard in other parts of what firms do.
I would advocate for raising this with your associates’ committee

kp.k: Bottom-up experimentation can support innovation and recruitment
kp.d: Leonard argues that junior lawyers’ task-level experience enables them to identify applications that experienced specialists may overlook, potentially generating efficiencies and new revenue streams. She also presents meaningful associate participation as a recruitment advantage where students struggle to distinguish firms. These are strategic recommendations and anticipated benefits, not measured innovation or hiring results.
qs: because this is such a weird technology, it also requires bottom-up learning.
The use cases are being developed at an individual level.
use cases that could create efficiencies or even open up new revenue streams for the firm that it hadn't thought of before.
To be perceived (or to actually be) the firm that is incorporating the voices of new talent into its future strategy, I think, is a smart recruitment tool as well.

kp.k: Mission-aligned frameworks should guide adaptation to rapid change
kp.d: Leonard advises leaders against trying to follow every development and instead recommends an organizational framework aligned with goals and mission, used to assess major developments and revised when necessary. McCormack says the AAA’s framework has been useful, while qualifying that the organization already had a sophisticated, well-resourced innovation program. The episode does not provide specific AAA implementation outcomes.
qs: it's a fool's errand to try to keep pace with the day-to-day, minute-to-minute developments.
create a framework that represents a strategy aligned with your organization's goals and mission.
when there are major developments, look back at that framework and consider how it applies and what decision would result—or adapt the framework as you go if things are changing so significantly.
I'm lucky that we already had a sophisticated, robust, well-resourced innovation program to be able to map all this onto.

kp.k: Strategy should address obsolescence, new capabilities, scale and competition
kp.d: McCormack offers four questions for legal-sector leaders, crediting Mollick with influencing her categorization: identify activities losing value, anticipate services newly becoming feasible, scale or open markets, and move work upmarket. She recommends maintaining a list of future capabilities and considering the time and people needed to realize them. These questions organize prospective strategy rather than document completed market changes.
qs: What do we do now that is no longer valuable, that people won't need because they can do it themselves or there are just going to be better, faster, cheaper ways to do it?
What can I not do today that I'm likely to be able to do tomorrow?
How do I democratize work and open new markets or grow current markets to a scale that wouldn't be possible today?
How do I move work upmarket so that I am competing in new ways?

kp.d: Leonard describes the billable hour as historically lucrative but constrained by finite human time. She predicts that AI will challenge highly leveraged global firms dependent on large volumes of junior billable hours and urges leaders to resist loss aversion and consider new markets. She does not quantify displacement, propose a specific alternative fee model or predict a particular future staffing shape.
qs: We've been so tethered to, at least in the private sector, the billable hour model for so long, and it's been a really successful, lucrative model for many firms, but it's also a huge limitation on what we're able to achieve.

really, really big global firms that are highly leveraged and rely on the generation of enormous amounts of billable hours at the junior levels in particular, will be impacted by this technology in ways that challenge their existing business model.

kp.k: Scaling legal services could address unmet civil needs
kp.d: Leonard identifies individuals and small businesses with unmet civil legal needs as a potential market for AI-enabled expansion. She states that 'something like 90%' of American civil legal needs go unmet, without identifying a study, denominator or period. Her argument is an anticipated access-to-justice opportunity, not evidence of an achieved reduction in unmet need.
qs: something like 90% of American civil legal needs go unmet.
That is an enormous untapped opportunity to serve small businesses and individuals, right?

kp.k: AI could strengthen smaller and resource-constrained legal providers
kp.d: Leonard predicts that AI can help solo and small practitioners, plaintiff-side lawyers, boutiques, public law departments and resource-deprived legal services organizations perform work previously beyond their capabilities and compete in new ways. McCormack also anticipates opportunities for courts and ADR providers, describing them as the legal system’s 'operating system' and crediting Jordan Furlong for that framing, but defers specific applications to a future episode.
qs: if you're a small or solo practitioner, if you're a plaintiff-side lawyer, if you're a boutique firm, if you're a public law department or a really resource-deprived legal services organization, this is such a game changer for you.
You can start to do things you weren't capable of doing, and really compete and transform the way that law is practiced.
ADR providers are like courts and judges; they're the operating system for the supply and the demand.

kp.k: Personal experimentation illustrates collaborative and personalized AI interactions
kp.d: McCormack’s account of correcting a cider itinerary illustrates her perception of AI as an iterative thought partner, while Leonard’s hotel query illustrates remembered context about her dog. McCormack also reports an unsolicited Pi message about a presentation, but only speculates that public information explained it. These personal anecdotes motivate their enthusiasm for broader applications; they do not establish legal reliability or the mechanism behind Pi’s behavior.
qs: But it included one cider place that was in a neighboring county.
It's not only going to give me information; it's going to work with me.
I know now there's memory stored, but the fact that it connected a pet question with that earlier conversation was really stunning to me.
there must have been some public-facing mention of this presentation.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Leonard predicts that connecting public legal research with firms’ internal work product will reduce duplication and information-switching; McCormack anticipates significant workflow and client-service changes.
pts.d: Leonard interprets the announced vLex–iManage partnership as an attempt to remove barriers between public legal materials and accumulated internal documents. She expects more such combinations. This is an interpretation of the partnership’s potential, not a report of measured efficiency gains or completed implementation.

pts.k: Leonard predicts that AI will reshape junior lawyers’ information-aggregation work and may affect associates’ work more than senior attorneys’ work.
pts.d: Drawing on her junior-associate experience, Leonard identifies switching between information sources, synthesis and aggregation as activities likely to become less central. She frames this as an opportunity to focus more on law itself, without predicting headcount reductions or specifying a replacement staffing structure.

pts.k: McCormack and Leonard argue that uneven, changing AI capabilities complicate legal adoption and can cause lawyers to abandon useful technology after an unsuccessful initial task.
pts.d: McCormack says AI is excellent at some tasks but unexpectedly weak at others, making experimentation necessary to identify useful applications. Leonard argues that lawyers receiving different results can mistakenly think they are debating the same experience. Both advocate repeated testing as capabilities change. Their discussion concerns task-dependent usefulness, not a quantified legal benchmark.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack argue that AI competence does not follow age or seniority automatically, and that adoption requires shared learning and experienced judgment.
pts.d: Leonard cites research involving BCG consultants as a challenge to the assumption that younger workers inherently know how best to deploy AI, then applies the implication to legal organizations. McCormack reports uneven enthusiasm among both senior professionals and younger people and sees an opportunity for intergenerational collaboration. The BCG research is cross-domain evidence, not a study of lawyers.

pts.k: McCormack claims that concealed employee AI use occurs despite organizational resistance and is riskier than guided use; Leonard predicts insurers or risk managers will encourage or require internal proprietary GPT systems.
pts.d: McCormack describes employees using AI without organizational guidance, potentially on personal devices, and argues that training and policies reduce the resulting risks. Leonard says AI detection is fallible and organizations cannot reliably identify AI-created work. Her forecast about insurers and risk managers is prospective, not a description of an existing requirement. The anecdote about a partner treating a typo as evidence of human authorship is reported as an anecdote, not established detection evidence.

pts.k: Leonard predicts that associate participation in AI adoption can generate efficiencies, new revenue opportunities and recruitment advantages; McCormack sees new opportunities for junior–senior collaboration.
pts.d: Leonard argues that individual experimentation and junior lawyers’ knowledge of their own tasks make bottom-up participation strategically important. She also predicts that firms incorporating junior voices will differentiate themselves in recruitment. McCormack frames AI initiatives as an unusual opportunity for new lawyers to work with senior colleagues outside conventional task hierarchies. These are strategic judgments rather than demonstrated revenue or recruitment results.

pts.k: Leonard predicts that AI will challenge large, highly leveraged firms’ junior-hour-dependent business models while creating opportunities to serve unmet civil legal needs.
pts.d: Leonard connects AI-driven change to the limits of selling lawyers’ time and to the reliance of large global firms on junior billable hours. She presents individuals and small businesses with unmet civil legal needs as a potential new market, conditional on organizations moving beyond loss aversion and exploring new services. Her approximate 90% unmet-need figure is offered without a citation or definition of the population measured.

pts.k: Leonard predicts that AI can help smaller and resource-constrained legal providers move upmarket and compete in ways previously unavailable to them.
pts.d: She explicitly includes solo and small practices, plaintiff-side lawyers, boutiques, public law departments and under-resourced legal services organizations. The proposed mechanism is expanded capability, not a specified product or demonstrated competitive outcome. McCormack likewise presents scaling, new offerings and moving upmarket as strategic possibilities, but her four-question framework is exploratory rather than evidence that these changes have already occurred.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The episode primarily supports its claims with professional experience, anecdotes, an announced vendor partnership and secondary accounts of research; it reports no quantified legal-AI performance results.
pts.d: For integration and junior-task changes, Leonard draws on the vLex–iManage announcement and her associate experience. For adoption barriers, McCormack relies on encounters with lawyers and explicitly says she read Mollick’s explanation rather than the underlying jagged-frontier paper. Leonard references recent BCG-consultant research without reporting methods, sample size or numerical findings. For concealed AI use, McCormack recounts a conference encounter with a resistant managing partner and nearby junior lawyers; Leonard explicitly says no secret user has personally disclosed such use to her. Recruitment claims draw on Leonard’s experience with law students. McCormack says the AAA strategy framework has been useful but defers operational examples to a later episode. The insurer forecast, new-revenue possibilities and competitive predictions are not supported with outcome data in this transcript.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2024 discussion mixes present adoption observations with largely undated near-term and longer-term forecasts.
pts.d: The partnership is recent news, while its workflow effects and additional combinations are prospective. Changes to associates’ roles and legal business models have no specified completion date. Capability boundaries are described as changing over days, weeks and months, requiring continuing experimentation. The BCG research is described as appearing 'last week, I think,' without a precise date. Leonard predicts insurer or risk-manager intervention 'very soon'; her separate 10–20-year reference describes a future retrospective on early AI bans, not the deadline for intervention. Market expansion is conditional on organizational willingness to experiment, address loss aversion and invest in implementation. McCormack qualifies her associate advice by noting that she is neither an associate nor working in a law firm.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ across junior lawyers, large firms, smaller providers, organizational leaders and underserved clients.
pts.d: Law-firm lawyers and clients may benefit from integrated information workflows. Associates face task redesign but may gain strategic influence and closer collaboration with senior lawyers. Leaders, employees and risk managers face governance challenges from undisclosed AI use and uneven literacy. Large global firms relying on many junior fee earners face pressure on billable-hour economics. Smaller practices, plaintiff-side lawyers, boutiques, public law departments and legal services organizations may gain capabilities and competitive reach. Individuals and small businesses unable to obtain civil legal help are identified as potential beneficiaries of expanded provision. Courts, judges and ADR providers receive an additional general statement of potential upside, but the episode defers concrete applications. vLex and iManage appear as technology vendors, not providers delivering alternative legal services.
